overall.basis: It is set against what has been written down somewhere a reader can check, not against everything that has happened. Three things hold it down. Whole scopes have had no research round yet. Countries whose courts and press do not publish leave almost nothing to find, so the thinnest parts of the map are often the places where the most is going on. And where someone has counted, as in the registers below, a single case on this map usually stands for many episodes underneath it.

benchmarks.name: Common Mechanisms of State Capture (Table 1)
benchmarks.publisher: Andreas Fiebelkorn — World Bank, Governance Global Practice Discussion Paper No. 2
benchmarks.scope: Classifies the mechanisms through which politically connected firms obtain advantages from the state, i.e. the policy and administrative levers by which business-state relationships are abused.
benchmarks.limits: It enumerates only the economic/regulatory levers that benefit politically connected firms and is built for quantitative measurement; it does not classify how the connection is established (lobbying, appointments, party funding, media) or capture by foreign states or non-commercial actors.

benchmarks.name: Policy Dystopia Model: taxonomy of instrumental strategies and techniques (Table 4)
benchmarks.publisher: Selda Ulucanlar, Gary J. Fooks, Anna B. Gilmore — PLoS Medicine 13(9): e1002125
benchmarks.scope: Classifies the instrumental techniques by which transnational tobacco companies act on policy makers and the policy process to prevent or weaken tobacco control legislation.
benchmarks.limits: It covers one industry's political activity against health regulation and is built from internal tobacco documents and interviews; it does not cover capture of courts, procurement, or public finance, nor outright bribery as a category, nor the separate taxonomy of discursive arguments the same paper publishes in Table 3.

benchmarks.name: Corporate political activity (CPA) strategies of the food industry
benchmarks.publisher: Melissa Mialon, Boyd Swinburn, Gary Sacks (Obesity Reviews, 2015), as printed in Table 1 of Mialon M & Mialon J, Public Health Nutrition 20(13)
benchmarks.scope: Classifies the strategies, with their named constituent practices, by which food industry actors seek to influence public health policy and the policy environment in their favour.
benchmarks.limits: It covers commercial actors' influence over health-related public policy using publicly available information; it does not cover covert or illicit capture (bribery of officials as a distinct type, judicial capture, procurement rigging), state or foreign-state actors, or capture of policy implementation.
